newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turk court begins trial of Islamic sect members.
newsitem.headline: Turk court begins trial of Islamic sect members.

text.p: Members of a fundamentalist Islamic sect in Turkey went on trial on Wednesday charged with seeking to overthrow the country's secular state, the semi-official Anatolian news agency said.

The 121 defendants from the Aczmendi group face three to five years in prison if convicted of insulting the founder of modern Turkey, Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, and forming a group aimed at destroying the state that he established.
"The Aczmendis, who claim Turkey is not governed in accordance with Islam, aim to create a state based on sharia (religious law)," state prosecutor Nuh Mete Yuksel told the courtroom.
The sect members were detained in October after clashing with police at an Islamist protest outside Ankara's main mosque.
Their sect has become a focus of lively media debate between Islamists and secularists since police in December detained its leader Muslum Gunduz, who now faces trial on similar charges.
He was captured naked in the company of a 24-year-old woman in a raid by police accompanied by televison crews. The woman has accused him of using religion to pressurise her into sex.
The start of Wednesday's trial was interrupted by a dispute over the Aczmendis' style of dress. They entered the courtroom dressed in their characteristic turbans and flowing dark robes.
The chief judge rejected an objection from another of the three judges who said their dress was an insult to the Turkish legal system.
Authorities in Turkey have long been wary of the group. Ataturk outlawed Islamic sects in the 1920s but the groups have quietly flourished again in recent years.

Turkey's first Islamist prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, came to power last June at the head of a coalition with conservatives. However, the form of Islam which he represents is far removed from that of the Aczmendis.
